main.text: It is proved that עזניה oznija is not the haliaeetus, as most hold, but the melanaeetus, or Valerian eagle.

Third among the unclean birds is עזניא oznija. The Greeks render it Ἁλιαίετον [Haliaieton], whence Jerome, Munster, Castalio, Pagninus, Arias, Junius and Diodati have haliaeetus or sea eagle; the English have ospray, which is the same; the Genevans have falcon, for what reason I do not well know, unless because some take the sea eagle for a falcon, whom, however, Gesner refutes. In the word עזניה oznija the Hebrews note that the Nun is נוסף, that is, epenthetic, and that עזניה oznija is said for עזיה ozja. Accordingly Onkelos here has עזיה ozja. And it is agreed that this species of eagle is so named from עוז oz, that is, strength. Hence I infer on very probable grounds that it is rather the μελαναίετον [melanaieton], that is, the black eagle, which, though the smallest of eagles, is nevertheless the strongest. For this reason the Romans call it Valeria, as being most powerful (valeat) in strength. Pliny, in the place cited above: "Called melanaeetos by the Greeks, and also Valeria, smallest in size, outstanding in strength, blackish in colour", etc. And before Pliny, the Philosopher, book 9, ch. 32: Ἕτερος δὲ μέλας τὴν χρόαν, καὶ μέγεθος ἐλάχιστος, καὶ κράτιστος τούτων. οὗτος οἰκεῖ ὄρη, καὶ ὕλας· καλεῖται δὲ μελαναίετος, καὶ λαγωφόνος. [Heteros de melas tēn chroan, kai megethos elachistos, kai kratistos toutōn. houtos oikei orē, kai hylas; kaleitai de melanaietos, kai lagōphonos.] "But there is another eagle, black in colour, smallest in [col. 189] size, but most excellent in strength. It inhabits mountains and forests, and is called melanaeetus" (that is, black eagle) "and hare-killer." And before the Philosopher, the greatest Poet, of Achilles, Iliad 21, line 252:
Αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων μέλανος, τοῦ θηρητῆρος· Ὅς θ᾽ ἅμα κάρτιστός τε, καὶ ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν· [Aietou oimat' echōn melanos, tou thērētēros; Hos th' hama kartistos te, kai ōkistos peteēnōn;]

"Having the onset of the black eagle, the hunter, which is at once the strongest and swiftest of birds." On this passage Eustathius: Αἰετοῦ μέλανος τῆς θηρητῆρος, ὃν καὶ μελαναίετόν τινες συνθέτως φασὶ, τὸν καὶ φασσοφόνον [Aietou melanos tēs thērētēros, hon kai melanaieton tines synthetōs phasi, ton kai phassophonon] (perhaps one should read λαγωφόνον [lagōphonon]) μικρὸν μέν φασιν ὄντα, τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἰσχυρότερον· [mikron men phasin onta, tōn allōn de ischyroteron;] "Of the black hunting eagle, which some call by a compound word melanaeetus, and dove-killer; small indeed, as they say, but stronger than the others." The old Scholiast of Homer writes that Aristotle, instead of μέλανος τοῦ [melanos tou], read with the words joined μελανόστου [melanostou], meaning that the eagle has black bones, and others μελανόσσου [melanossou], as if with black eyes. But in the extant books of Aristotle nothing similar occurs. And the Poet's reading is tampered with in vain, for it is apt and learned, and brings him into agreement with Aristotle and Pliny in describing the black eagle. Since, then, by their consensus the black eagle is the strongest of all, why should it not have been called עזניה osnija by the Hebrews from its strength, as valeria by the Romans? Moreover, it is not at all likely [II, 775] that this species was omitted by Moses among the eagles, since after that greater and genuine eagle, properly called נשר, this is the most noteworthy (ἀξιομνημονεύτατος [axiomnēmoneutatos]) of all eagles. For besides its exceptional strength it has very many qualities that especially commend it. The Philosopher describes them thus in the place cited: Ἐκτρέφει δὲ μόνος οὗτος τὰ τέκνα, καὶ ἐξάγει· ἔστι δὲ ὠκυβόλος, καὶ εὐθήμων, καὶ ἄφθονος, καὶ ἄφοβος, καὶ μάχιμος, καὶ εὔφημος· οὐ γὰρ μινυρίζει, οὐδὲ λέληκεν. [Ektrephei de monos houtos ta tekna, kai exagei; esti de ōkybolos, kai euthēmōn, kai aphthonos, kai aphobos, kai machimos, kai euphēmos; ou gar minyrizei, oude lelēken.] "This one alone rears and brings out its young. It is also swift, elegant, without envy, without fear, vigorous, of good omen; it neither screams nor murmurs." Accordingly the most distinguished Thuanus, book 1 De re accipitraria, compares it with the chrysaetus thus:

"Excellent, she too equals that one in mighty spirit, though she is inferior in bulk of body, and not so strong in talon, beak or toes; but, not belying her birth nor forgetful of a manly spirit, she makes hawks look bastard by comparison. Her too our people call Valeria, the Greeks μελαναίετον [melanaieton], because in beak, feathers and talon she shows a dark colour" ^{(1)}.

It should be noted that both עזניה oznija and פרס peres are taken by some for the griffin, and that accordingly both are rendered עוז uz or עוזא uza, a word that among the paraphrasts and the Talmudists means griffin. Thus in Jonathan's paraphrase עוזא uza stands for פרס peres, while in the Samaritan ࠏࠅࠆࠀ uza stands for ࠏࠆࠍࠉࠄ oznija. And in the Talmudic tractate Kelim, ch. 17, § 14, where vessels made מכנף העוז, from the wing of the uz, that is, of the griffin, are discussed, the Glossator has this: עוף הוא ששמו עזניה ורגילים היו לעשות כלים מכנף אותו העוז, It is a bird which (in the sacred text) is called oznija, from whose wings vessels used to be made. Here perhaps instead of מכנף miccanaph (from the wing) we should read מכף miccaph (from the sole). And shortly after, כף העוז מכל הכפים, The sole (of the bird) uz surpasses every other, instead of כנף העוז מכל הכנפים, The wing of the bird uz surpasses every wing. Sole, that is, foot and talon; for that is what כף caph means in birds. So Gen. VIII, 9. The dove found no rest לכף רגלה: and Erpenianus has لكف رجلها [li-kaff rijlihā] for the sole of her foot, that is, τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῆς [tois posin autēs], for her feet, as the Greeks have there. Moreover, they commonly say that vessels are made from the griffin's feet or talons, not from its wings. Damir, in the chapter On [col. 190] عنقا [ʿanqā] anka, or the Griffin: فيصنع من مخاليبها اقداح [II, 776] عظام للشرب [fa-yuṣnaʿ min makhālībihā aqdāḥ ʿiẓām li-l-shurb] And from its talons large drinking vessels are made. Gesner, on the griffin: John Mandeville writes that its talons are like the horns of an ox, from which cups of great value are made. And shortly after: I remember seeing at a goldsmith's in our city a smooth black horn, hooked at the top, almost as in chamois, perhaps three times as thick, whose rim the goldsmith was about to mount in silver, so that it might be used as a cup at table. It was perhaps the horn of some foreign ox, such as the one they call Indian, or of a buffalo. But he had received it as a griffin's talon. I shall adduce another testimony showing that עזניה oznija is the griffin in the opinion of the Hebrews. In the book בעל החיים, or On the Natures of Animals, which Calonymus translated from the Arabic of Abulsapha into Hebrew, the עזניה oznija, ruling far and wide over the birds of prey, summons them from every side and speaks thus in their council: הנה אני עם גודל גופי ואומץ כוחי ומהירות עופפותי עזבתי בתיהם וברחתי מהם אל האיים הרחוקים ואל ההרים הרמים והנשואים, I indeed, though vast in body, outstanding in strength and swift of wing, have left their (men's) dwellings and fled from them to remote islands and to steep and lofty mountains. Not very differently Maimonides on the peres and the oznija, in the tractate On Forbidden Foods, ch. 1, § 17: פרס ועזניה אינן מצויין בישוב אלא במדברות איי הים הרחוקות עד מאד שהן סוף הישוב, The Perez and the oznija are not found in the inhabited world (ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ [en tē oikoumenē]), but in the most remote islands of the sea at the farthest edge of the world. It is obvious that this refers to the anca of the Arabs, or griffin, which they fable once lived among men in Arabia and fed on beasts and birds; but when it had once carried off children and even a bride, it was banished at the prayers of the Prophet Handala to an island most remote from human intercourse, from which it is forbidden to come out to betake itself to more cultivated places. Accordingly, for the Hebrew עזניה oznija one reads in the Arabic paraphrases, of Saadia as of others, العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka. And for this reason Aben Ezra is angry with Saadia for holding that God forbade הדבר שלא היה, a thing that does not exist. The Arabs themselves admit this. Among them is Alcamus, by whom العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka is defined with an elegant paronomasia as طاير معروف الاسم ومجهول الجسم [ṭāʾir maʿrūf al-ism wa-majhūl al-jism], a bird of known alism, that is, name, but unknown algism, that is, body. And the poet who says الجود والغول والعنقا ثلاثة اسما اشيا لم توجد ولم تكن [al-jūd wa-l-ghūl wa-l-ʿanqā thalātha asmā ashyā lam tūjad wa-lam takun] Liberality, and algol (or empusa) and alanca (or griffin) are three names of things that are not found and exist nowhere. But elsewhere I show that Saadia and the other paraphrasts who use this word can be excused, because, although anca is mostly the name of a fictitious bird, as griffins are for us, yet it sometimes also occurs for a real bird. But whatever they had in mind, this is certain: עזניה oznija in Moses signifies a real bird, and very probably it is the black eagle, which the Greeks call by the compound word μελαναίετον [melanaieton].

notes.text: You will find the synonyms of the Valerian eagle in Linn. Syst. T. I. vol. I. p. 254, no. 2, under this name: Falco cera lutea pedibusque semilanatis, corpore e ferrugineo nigricante, striis flavis [falcon with yellow cere and half-woolly feet, body blackish from rust-colour, with yellow streaks]. Other conjectures, but less probable, in my opinion, were put forward by Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1880. These too rest on etymologies alone,
